title: Synthetic integration-test fixture

supported_claims.claim: The ILO assesses potential generative AI exposure using occupation tasks and distinguishes different degrees of exposure across occupations.

Global research is not direct evidence of Malaysian employer demand or AI adoption.

reuse_conditions: Provide appropriate attribution and identify adaptations.
notes: Supporting research for task-exposure and uncertainty methodology, not an occupation-specific Malaysian AI displacement forecast.

title: O*NET 31.0 Database — Skills and Occupational Tasks
publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA); National Center for O*NET Development
report_period: O*NET 31.0 (August 2026); individual occupation measurements have different dates
evidence_location: Skills (IM and LV) and Task Ratings/Task Statements for six representative O*NET-SOC occupations; observe record-specific Date and Recommend Suppress flags

supported_claims.claim: O*NET publishes general-skill importance (IM) ratings for US occupations; the project converts only directly matched, unsuppressed values using its own proposed 1–4 mapping.
Published O*NET occupational tasks support relevance of selected project skills but their task importance ratings are not numerical skill-importance ratings.
supported_claims.evidence_location: O*NET Task Statements and Task Ratings; data/processed/onet_task_skill_evidence.json

limitations: O*NET-SOC occupations are US occupation profiles and not an official Malaysian MASCO crosswalk.

The team-defined 1–4 weight conversion is not an official O*NET score.
Task importance is not skill importance; neither estimates AI displacement or Malaysian labour-market demand.

reuse_conditions: Credit the source and link the CC BY 4.0 licence.
Clearly identify project adaptations and derived indicators.

title: The OECD AI exposure measure: Mapping the OECD AI Capability Indicators to occupations
publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
geography: United States O*NET-SOC occupation mapping; OECD research
evidence_location: OECD AI Capability Gap Index public workbook (README, Data, Scenario, Codebook); reversed normalized index (AI Capability Gap Index_Rev. norm.)

supported_claims.claim: The OECD reversed normalized AI Capability Gap Index is a research measure of overlap between occupation capability requirements and AI capabilities, not the likelihood of losing a job.
supported_claims.evidence_location: Workbook Codebook and Data sheets; OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 59

supported_claims.claim: The workbook Scenario sheet explores a hypothetical one-level increase in selected AI cognitive capabilities; it is not a date-specific adoption prediction.
supported_claims.evidence_location: Workbook README, Scenario and Codebook sheets

limitations: Exposure index is not a job-loss/replacement probability, Malaysian adoption rate, salary prediction or guaranteed future outcome.
Four of the six project O*NET codes matched exactly in the supplied workbook; Software Developers and Data Professionals remain null.
OECD one-level cognitive capability scenario is not equivalent to SkillShift AI moderate/fast adoption scenarios.
The original OECD index has been kept separate from team-selected career skill weights.
attribution: OECD (2026), “The OECD AI exposure measure: Mapping the OECD AI Capability Indicators to occupations”, OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers, No. 59, OECD Publishing, Paris, https://doi.org/10.1787/f3da0f0a-en. Project extraction and presentation are adaptations.
reuse_conditions: Credit the source and link the CC BY 4.0 licence.
Clearly identify project adaptations and derived indicators.

data_files.role: Processed OECD baseline and research-scenario indicators for six mapped project careers
data_files.evidence_level: Four exact US O*NET-SOC matches; two explicit missing values

notes: OECD workbook README lists the full dataset at https://aicapabilityindicators.oecd.org/publications.html and states CC BY 4.0.
The baseline indicator is best displayed as an index out of 1, not as a percentage of jobs replaced.
Original workbook kept outside the processed application source registry file paths because local workbook placement can vary.

title: The Future of Jobs Report 2025
evidence_location: Executive summary and Section 3: Skills outlook

supported_claims.claim: Surveyed global employers expect AI and big data, cybersecurity and technological literacy skills to grow in importance.
Analytical thinking, creative thinking and other human-centred capabilities remain important or are expected to grow.
Employers expect an average of 39% of existing skill sets to be transformed or become outdated during 2025–2030.

limitations: Global employer expectations are not measured Malaysian skill demand.
The report does not provide numeric readiness multipliers for SkillShift AI skills.
WEF skill categories are not identical to our 36 skill IDs.
attribution: World Economic Forum (2025), The Future of Jobs Report 2025.
reuse_conditions: Attribute and paraphrase; do not redistribute the report without licence review.
notes: Global employer-expectations report, not Malaysian observed hiring or a source of measured skill multipliers.
